questions.text: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python, and when would you use each?
questions.reference_answer: Lists are mutable so elements can be changed, added or removed after creation, while tuples are immutable and cannot be modified. Because tuples are immutable and hashable they can be used as dictionary keys or set elements, which lists cannot. Use a list for a collection that changes, and a tuple for a fixed record such as coordinates.

concepts.name: mutability
concepts.explanation: lists are mutable, tuples are immutable

concepts.name: hashability
concepts.explanation: tuples can be dict keys because they are hashable

concepts.name: use cases
concepts.explanation: choose by whether data should change

follow_ups.hashability: Why can a tuple be used as a dictionary key but a list cannot?
follow_ups.mutability: What happens if you try to assign to an element of a tuple?

questions.text: Explain INNER JOIN versus LEFT JOIN in SQL with an example of when each is appropriate.
questions.reference_answer: An inner join returns only rows that have matching values in both tables. A left join returns every row from the left table and the matching rows from the right table, filling the right-side columns with NULL where there is no match. Use an inner join when you only want matched records, and a left join when you must keep all records from the left table, for example all customers including those with no orders.

concepts.name: inner join matches only
concepts.explanation: inner join keeps only matched rows

concepts.name: left join keeps all left rows
aliases: all the rows from the left
concepts.explanation: left join keeps all left rows

misconceptions.explanation: A left join keeps all left rows, not only matching ones.
An inner join returns only matched rows.

follow_ups.null for unmatched: What value do unmatched right-side columns take in a LEFT JOIN, and how would you filter for them?

questions.text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
questions.reference_answer: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation happens, so it cannot use aggregate functions like SUM or COUNT. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has aggregated the rows, so it can use aggregate functions. For example, WHERE selects orders from 2025, then GROUP BY customer, then HAVING keeps customers whose total is above 1000.

concepts.name: where filters rows before grouping
concepts.explanation: WHERE acts on rows before aggregation

concepts.name: having filters groups after aggregation
concepts.explanation: HAVING acts on groups after aggregation

misconceptions.explanation: WHERE cannot filter on aggregates; HAVING does.

questions.text: What is overfitting in machine learning, why does it happen, and how can you reduce it?
questions.reference_answer: Overfitting is when a model learns the training data too closely, including noise, so it performs well on training data but poorly on unseen data. It happens when the model is too complex for the amount of data, or the data is noisy or small. It can be reduced with more data, a simpler model, regularization, cross-validation, early stopping or dropout.

concepts.name: poor generalisation
concepts.explanation: good on training data, bad on unseen data

misconceptions.explanation: Overfitting is good training performance with poor performance on unseen data.

follow_ups.remedies: Pick one technique to reduce overfitting and explain why it works.
follow_ups.poor generalisation: How would you detect overfitting from training and validation curves?

questions.text: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.
questions.reference_answer: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions, which causes underfitting. Variance is error from sensitivity to the particular training data, which causes overfitting. Making a model more complex typically lowers bias but raises variance, so you look for the complexity that minimises total error on unseen data.

concepts.name: trade-off with complexity
concepts.explanation: complexity lowers bias but raises variance

misconceptions.explanation: High bias corresponds to underfitting; high variance to overfitting.

questions.text: What are precision and recall, and why can accuracy be misleading on imbalanced data?
questions.reference_answer: Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive, TP divided by TP plus FP. Recall is the fraction of actual positives that the model finds, TP divided by TP plus FN. On imbalanced data a model that always predicts the majority class can have high accuracy but zero recall, so precision, recall and F1 give a better picture, and there is a trade-off controlled by the decision threshold.

concepts.name: accuracy misleading when imbalanced
concepts.explanation: accuracy can be high while missing the minority class

misconceptions.explanation: Precision uses false positives in the denominator; recall uses false negatives.

questions.text: Why do we split data into training and test sets, and what is data leakage?
questions.reference_answer: We hold out a test set that the model never sees during training so we can estimate how it performs on unseen data. Data leakage is when information from the test or future data influences training, for example scaling using statistics from the whole dataset, which makes results look better than they will be in practice. Hyperparameters are tuned on a validation set or with cross-validation, and the test set is used once at the end.

concepts.name: held-out unseen data
concepts.explanation: test set estimates performance on unseen data

concepts.name: data leakage
concepts.explanation: test information influencing training inflates results

misconceptions.explanation: Tuning on the test set leaks information; use a validation set.

questions.text: What does a p-value tell you in a hypothesis test?
questions.reference_answer: The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what we saw, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value, below a chosen significance level such as 0.05, is evidence against the null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the size or importance of an effect.

concepts.name: probability under the null
concepts.explanation: p-value is computed assuming the null is true

concepts.name: as extreme or more extreme data
concepts.explanation: probability of data at least as extreme

misconceptions.explanation: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

questions.text: When would you report the median instead of the mean?
questions.reference_answer: The mean is sensitive to outliers and skewed data, while the median is robust because it depends only on the middle value. For skewed data such as incomes or house prices, the median better represents a typical value, so I would report the median or both.

concepts.name: outlier sensitivity
concepts.explanation: mean is sensitive to outliers; median is robust

concepts.name: skewed distributions
concepts.explanation: median represents typical value in skewed data

misconceptions.explanation: The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is robust.

questions.text: What is a closure in JavaScript and what is it useful for?
questions.reference_answer: A closure is a function together with the variables from its surrounding lexical scope that it keeps access to even after the outer function has returned. Closures are useful for private state such as counters, for callbacks and event handlers, and for function factories.

concepts.name: lexical scope retention
concepts.explanation: inner function keeps access to outer variables

concepts.name: persists after outer returns
concepts.explanation: access persists after the outer function returns

questions.text: Describe the main HTTP methods used in a REST API and what each is for.
questions.reference_answer: GET reads a resource and is safe and idempotent. POST creates a new resource and is not idempotent. PUT replaces a resource and is idempotent, PATCH partially updates it, and DELETE removes it. Responses use status codes such as 200 for success, 201 for created and 404 for not found.

misconceptions.explanation: GET should only read; it must not change data.

questions.text: What is the difference between props and state in React?
questions.reference_answer: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child and are read-only for the child. State is data owned and managed inside a component that can change over time, and updating it with useState or setState triggers a re-render. Data flows one way, from parent to child through props.

concepts.name: props passed from parent, read-only
concepts.explanation: props are read-only inputs from the parent

misconceptions.explanation: A child must not modify its props.

questions.text: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
questions.reference_answer: Merge combines branches by creating a merge commit and preserves the original history. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history to produce a linear history. Because rebase rewrites commits, you should not rebase branches that others have already pulled.

concepts.name: merge commit preserves history
concepts.explanation: merge preserves history with a merge commit

concepts.name: rebase rewrites for linear history
concepts.explanation: rebase replays commits to give linear history

questions.text: How does a hash table work, and what happens when two keys collide?
questions.reference_answer: A hash table applies a hash function to a key to compute an index into an array of buckets, giving average O(1) lookup, insertion and deletion. When two keys hash to the same index that is a collision, handled by chaining, where each bucket holds a list, or by open addressing, which probes for another slot. In the worst case with many collisions, operations degrade to O(n).

concepts.name: hash function to index
concepts.explanation: hash function maps key to a bucket index

concepts.name: collision handling
concepts.explanation: collisions resolved by chaining or probing

misconceptions.explanation: O(1) is the average case; the worst case is O(n).

questions.text: What is database normalization and why is it used?
questions.reference_answer: Normalization organises tables to reduce redundancy and avoid insert, update and delete anomalies, using normal forms such as 1NF, 2NF and 3NF. The trade-off is that more joins are needed, so some systems denormalize selected tables to improve read performance.

questions.text: Explain the four pillars of object-oriented programming.
questions.reference_answer: Encapsulation bundles data and methods and hides internal details behind an interface. Abstraction exposes only essential behaviour. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class. Polymorphism lets different classes be used through the same interface with different behaviour.

concepts.name: encapsulation
concepts.explanation: bundle data and methods, hide details

questions.text: You receive a messy dataset. What steps do you take to clean it before analysis?
questions.reference_answer: I first profile the data to see types, ranges and missing values. I handle missing values by imputing or dropping depending on how much is missing and why, remove duplicates, fix inconsistent formats and categories, and investigate outliers rather than deleting them blindly. Then I validate the result against known totals and document every change so the work is reproducible.

misconceptions.explanation: Outliers should be investigated, not removed blindly.

questions.text: How do you choose an appropriate chart type for a dataset?
questions.reference_answer: I start from the question being answered. Bar charts compare categories, line charts show trends over time, scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric variables, and histograms show distributions. I avoid cluttered or 3D charts, label axes and units, and keep the audience in mind.

concepts.name: start from the question
concepts.explanation: choice depends on the question and audience

concepts.name: chart-to-task mapping
concepts.explanation: bar for categories, line for time, scatter for relationships
